12.2 Facebook User Displeasure Actually Leads to Less, but Better Organic Content

At this stage, according to Social Flow, organic reach was still dropping at a rate of 42% between January and May of 20161.  Ironically, however, Facebook users noticed the trend of more and more ad content in their timeline news feeds, along with a plethora of uninteresting, low-quality organic posts.  Through both, Facebook users began voicing their displeasure as posts from businesses, brands, and media were crowding out the personal moments that led users to connect more with each other in the first place2.  Facebook realized they had to fix this saturation issue by changing the algorithm.  They needed to promote high-quality, personalized content to continue building meaningful relationships in the social space.

In the blog post announcing the algorithm change, Facebook Engineering Director Lars Backstrom indicated the new algorithm update would try to ensure that “stories posted directly by friends that you care about, such as photos, videos, status updates or links, will be higher up in the News Feed, so you are less likely to miss them.”  He also warned that Pages could anticipate a dip in organic reach and referral traffic for some pages and encouraged Pages to post things they know their audiences are likely to share with their friends3.  With this change, Social Flow adjusted their original report from 42% to a decrease of 52% from January to July of 20164.

Furthermore, Facebook doubled down on this commitment to friends and family in the next two years.  In 2017, Facebook did not change the algorithm but rather changed the News Feed function entirely.  In October, Facebook tested an ad-free News Feed that users could switch to, dedicated to publisher content rather than personal content. To businesses, it clearly foreshadowed a Facebook that separated business/brand content from friends/family content.  Today, that "alternative News Feed" is known as the "Pages" option on the left-hand sidebar of a user's News Feed5.

In 2018, Facebook again updated its News Feed algorithm.  This update did not eliminate Page content entirely but set different priorities on what would be posted to users’ News Feed.  Paul Armstrong provides a great article about a Facebook webinar that shared these priorities at Forbes.com6.  He highlights what Facebook prioritizes as important for News Feeds:

  • People sharing a link over Messenger
  • Commenting on or liking a person's photo or status updates
  • Multiple replies to a status update or photo = more likely to see again
  • Meaningful interactions - this doesn't mean 'like if you agree.'

He also notes that Facebook wants content publishers to have other people share their content with Facebook and not be the initial publisher of the content.  That means content creation on blog sites needs to have social posts buttons that allow users to post into space rather than posting it directly into the social space.  Facebook also provided additional tips for content publishers from this webinar.

Additional Tips for Content Publishers:

  • Have other people share your content on Facebook.
  • Start getting journalists to comment and spur on activity.
  • Focus on content that other people will share.
  • Create stories that can be updated.
  • Use paid media to create spikes on relevant content.
  • Start thinking about local products.
  • Start pushing the 'Follow' function for Pages.
  • Stop tagging.
  • Become engaged in Facebook Groups.

Finally, shares and comments, in particular, are considered "active" interactions, which Facebook considers more "meaningful" when slotting content on a user's News Feed. For that reason, video watch time, referral traffic, and organic reach might even decrease this year if the content does not create a meaningful interaction7.

 

References:

1. Social Flow.  Media Companies’ Facebook Reach Has Fallen 42% This Year.  http://www.socialflow.com/media-companies-facebook-reach-has-fallen-42-this-year/

2. NeilPatel.com.  Is Facebook Organic Reach Really Dead?  Here’s How to Break Through It for More Social Engagement.  https://neilpatel.com/blog/is-facebook-organic-reach-dead/

3. Facebook Newsroom.  Helping Make Sure You Don’t Miss Stories from Friends.  https://newsroom.fb.com/news/2016/06/news-feed-fyi-helping-make-sure-you-dont-miss-stories-from-friends/

4. MarketingLand.com.  Facebook Organic Reach Is Down 52% for Publishers’ Pages This Year.  https://marketingland.com/facebook-organic-reach-drop-steepens-52-publishers-pages-187253

5. HubSpot.  The Decline of Organic Facebook Reach & How to Adjust to the Algorithm.  https://blog.hubspot.com/marketing/facebook-organic-reach-declining

12.3 Strategic Approaches to Declining Organic Facebook Reach

The “Reachpocalypse” of 2014 was the peak of the online debate on whether or not organic reach was dead.  And even though digital media agencies have continued to demonstrate the decline of organic reach on Facebook across their clients, Nic Robertson of agency Bonsey Jaden contends that organic reach still exists in 20182.  Bonsey Jaden demonstrates that the global average in 2014 was as low as 2.11% for brands, but some of their best-performing Facebook Pages remained above 3% reach four years later.  The takeaway from Bonsey Jaden is that it has not reached 0% and has slowed down or reversed from some of the best-performing brands.  The question at hand is, what makes these best-performing brands continue to see organic reach?

1. The overwhelming consensus is to focus on quality, not quantity.  

Whether it’s Bonsey Jaden, Neil Patel, or Facebook themselves, the appropriate strategic approach is to spend more time on a few pieces of well-thought-out content with a brand-supportive message.  A recent case study produced by Buffer3 demonstrates this point.  From January through October of 2016, Buffer was posting between 3-5 Facebook posts per day.  However, the data showed that the more they posted to Facebook, the less reach they received on each post, especially during peak posting times.  However, in October of that year, when Buffer started experimenting with the posting strategy, they realized that fewer posts were actually leading to higher reach numbers and more Facebook engagement, as seen in the series of graphs below.

2. Educate your Facebook Page followers on how to see your posts more often. 

There are various areas in which you can educate your followers on seeing and engaging with your content more frequently.  First, remind your followers that they can always go to the Pages Feed on the left sidebar of their News Feed to see content from pages they have “Liked,” including yours.  Next, super fans can always change their notification settings to see your posts first on their News Feed.  This option is located in the “Following” drop-down menu just under your Page picture (as seen below).  Finally, remind your followers to engage with your posts when they see them so they will see them more and more often.

3. Engage in the new features on Facebook.

Facebook is putting more emphasis on the newer components of the platform, including video and Facebook Live.  A recent study by Quintly4 demonstrated that native Facebook videos are shared more than 1000% more than videos linked from other hosting sites.  They also have a 186% higher engagement rate, 530% more comments, and accumulated over 89% of the overall video posts on Facebook.  Wow!  The overwhelming takeaway here is that the Facebook algorithm highly favors videos directly uploaded to Facebook.  It is highly recommended to only use videos you directly upload to Facebook as other formats generally receive much lower engagement than Facebook Native videos.

Additionally, if you're not already doing so, start broadcasting on Facebook Live.  According to HubSpot5, users spend three times more time watching live broadcasts than traditional videos on the platform.  To use it effectively, Hubspot5 suggests you advertise what you're doing on different platforms to generate buzz, broadcast for several minutes (at least) to help your broadcast surfaced in the News Feed, and share authentic behind-the-scenes content to attract and interest your viewers.

4. Research the best time to post to Facebook.

The rumors are true.  There is an optimal time of day to post to Facebook when your audience is most likely to be on Facebook.  To measure the most active time of day for your target audience, click on your Facebook Insights tab in the top menu on Facebook.  Then in the left-hand sidebar, click on posts, as demonstrated in the example below.  The “When Your Fans are Online” function at the top of this Insights Posts page will help you determine when your Facebook audience is online during the day.  As you can see from the information below, of the roughly 2400 fans that this website has, most fans (1258) are on Facebook during the 8 pm hour of the evening.  However, after the 9 pm hour, the number of users precipitously drops off.  We recommend posting on this channel at 7 pm and letting the post run through 7-10 pm peak hours.  Knowing when to post is important for optimizing your organic reach.

5. Consider joining Facebook Groups as a potential long-term solution to organic reach.

In June of 2017, Mark Zuckerberg announced a revised mission for Facebook at the first-ever Facebook Communities Summit in Chicago.  He proclaimed that over the next decade, Facebook would “Give people the power to build community and bring the world closer together.”  Strategically, this announcement was made in front of hundreds of group admins invited to this community summit.  Zuckerberg stated that an important part of delivering this new mission is supporting the formation of Facebook Groups and supporting those group administrators.  This support included adding Group Insights, real-time metrics for group admins to monitor growth, engagement, and membership of the group’s superfans.  With this emphasis, more than one billion people worldwide now use Groups. More than 100 million people consider themselves members of “meaningful groups” that are becoming the most important part of their Facebook experience6.  As Neil Patel states, Facebook’s groups “could be the ultimate answer to the Organic Search issue.”7

6. Grow Your Organic Traffic with paid Likes Campaign

Growing your followers and Likes is the next best thing to email. This is true if we talk about Facebook, Instagram, Twitter, Linked In, or any other platform. More Likes or Followers are the ones you will connect and engage with, and they will expand your Reach.

We have consistently seen a dramatic impact from running paid campaigns to attract more followers. Unlike post boost or paid ads, this campaign adds more followers that will continue to grow. Properly targeted and balanced will be a highly successful way to grow your brand reach and engagement. It will also offset any attrition you have from followers unfollowing or leaving the platform.

Paid Likes Campaign:

  • Start by spending a small monthly budget on Facebook Likes ads to grow your followers and organic reach.
  • Growing Likes is the next best thing to email. Swiftwick grew Likes by over 307%, adding over 3,743 in 30 days.
  • Likes campaign will open more walls expanding your organic post reach. Swiftwick Reach was up 91% in this period and continued to grow.
  • Swiftwick Likes increased to over 100,000, and Reach rose to over 5 million monthly.

7. Supplement your organic traffic with a Facebook pay-to-play strategy.

A final strategy to help your Facebook Page deal with declining organic reach is to consider a pay-to-play approach.  Spending even nominal amounts on Facebook will help elevate your normal organic reach baseline.  For example, view the hub and spoke the results below.  In the Facebook Overview analytics on the bottom, one will notice two distinct spikes in Facebook reach.  The first on September 18th was an organic spike, while the second spike on September 28th was a paid spike (e.g., boosted post).  Notice how the baseline for Facebook Reach (red line) increased from an average daily reach of about 600 before the spike to roughly 1300 after the spike.  Likewise, after the paid spike the baseline average went up even more to about 2000 in reach.  This is not an atypical occurrence on Facebook.  Whether purchasing ads, boosting posts, or starting a Likes campaign, all nominal spending within the Facebook platform will open up additional reach for your page.  As witnessed below, while having a very successful organic spike, you never know which day or post will come.   But ad buys within Facebook will always open up additional reach.  This is the essence of pay-to-play, and why Facebook’s ad revenue is more than 60% greater than YouTube, it’s the next closest competitor in ad revenue (see Chapter 9).

 

References:

1. Convince & Convert.  This Chart Explains the Reachpocalypse and Why Facebook is Laughing All the Way to the Bank.  https://www.convinceandconvert.com/social-media-tools/this-chart-explains-the-reachpocalypse-and-why-facebook-is-laughing-all-the-way-to-the-bank/

2. Bonsey Jaden.  The Truth About Facebook Organic Reach in 2018.  https://bonseyjaden.com/truth-facebook-organic-reach-2018/

3. Buffer.  The Simple Facebook Posting Strategy That Helped us 3x Our Reach and Engagement.  https://blog.bufferapp.com/facebook-posting-strategy

4. Quintly. Study Proves 530% more comments on Facebook Native videos.  https://www.quintly.com/blog/2017/03/facebook-video-study

5. HubSpot.  The Decline of Organic Facebook Reach & How to Adjust to the Algorithm.  https://blog.hubspot.com/marketing/facebook-organic-reach-declining

6. Facebook Newsroom.  Our First Communities Summit and New Tolls for Group Admins.  https://newsroom.fb.com/news/2017/06/our-first-communities-summit-and-new-tools-for-group-admins/

7. NeilPatel.com.  Is Facebook Organic Reach Really Dead?  Here’s How to Break Through It for More Social Engagement.  https://neilpatel.com/blog/is-facebook-organic-reach-dead/

12.4 Additional Social Media Channel Insights

We will not go into each social media channel's critical history and details that you may or may not use in your live campaigns.  However, HubSpot, SemRush, and other tools provide immense content on the most popular of these channels over the years.  If you are using any of these social media channels in your campaign, then we highly suggest you click on the logo to read about successful strategies for each channel that you are using.  There is some great content on each of these channels from Hubspot.

 

 

 

While insights at the individual channels may be helpful, they vary widely between channels and make it difficult to determine the real impact of your campaigns. You want to make sure you are growing your audience and impacting your audience within each channel you are working on. However, the most important thing is the referral traffic to your website. Having a large following and getting interactions is great, but if the audience is not clicking through to your website, you are not creating the engagement and relationship to grow your brand. For example, Instagram makes it difficult to get traffic through to your website unless you buy ads. You will constantly have to remind your audience to click on the link in your Instagram Profile.

Our program is platform-agnostic, meaning that it is independent of any open single platform. We have seen our clients and students run very successful campaigns regardless of the social channels they choose to utilize. We only showed Facebook as an in-depth example to demonstrate the importance of what to do and the desired results regardless of the social channels. Keep the main thing, the main thing, and make sure you are successfully working each channel and that they are contributing Referral traffic back to your website. If not, continue to tweak the messaging to improve the results with your channels before adding any new ones.

This is why we report Social Referrals from Google Analytics to the top of your Dashboard on your website every week.

Knowing where your traffic is coming from at the top level is one of your most important Dashboard indicators.

To "peek" under the Dashboard and see how each Social Channel is performing, go to Google Analytics > Acquisition > All Traffic > Channels and then click on Social in the report to see how each channel is performing in delivering Referral Traffic by Social Channel.

13.1 Email Reporting

When navigating to an email report, you are generally looking to find how a general campaign is functioning regarding clicks, opens, total revenue generated (if possible), and how many unsubscribes or abuse reports may have been filed with each other email in the campaign.  Specifically, MailChimp campaign reports look like this:

The following metrics of this report are detailed below1:

  • Recipients
    Number of subscribers the campaign was sent to.
  • Delivered
    Date and time the campaign completed sending from Mailchimp servers.
  • Open rate
    Percentage of successfully delivered campaigns that registered as an open.
  • Click rate
    Percentage of successfully delivered campaigns that registered a click.
  • List average for opens and clicks
    Average percentage of opens or clicks on previous campaigns sent to this list.
  • Industry average for opens and clicks
    Average percentage of opens or clicks for campaigns in the selected industry set for your account.
  • Opened
    Number of recipients that opened this campaign any number of times.
  • Clicked
    Number of recipients that clicked any tracked link any number of times in this campaign.
  • Bounced
    Number of recipients that registered as a hard or soft bounce.
  • Unsubscribed
    Number of subscribers that opted out of your list using the unsubscribe link in this campaign.
  • Total opens
    Total number of times recipients opened the campaign. This count includes multiple opens from individual recipients.
  • Successful deliveries
    The number of recipients that didn't hard or soft bounce on this campaign.
  • Clicks per unique opens
    Percentage of recipients that registered as an open who also clicked a link in your campaign.
  • Total clicks
    Total number of times tracked links were clicked by recipients. This count includes multiple clicks from individual recipients.
  • Forwarded
    Number of times the campaign was forwarded using the Forward to a Friend form. This stat considers forwards only through the Forward to a Friend form and cannot detect when a subscriber uses the forwarding function in their email program.
  • Forward opens
    Number of times the campaign was opened by someone who has forwarded the campaign using a Forward to a Friend form.
  • Abuse reports
    Number of recipients that reported your email as spam. Subscribers that report a campaign as spam are automatically unsubscribed from your list.
  • Last opened
    The most recent instance of a recipient opening the campaign.
  • Last clicked
    The most recent instance of a recipient clicking a tracked link in the campaign.
  • 24-hour performance
    A graph detailing subscriber activity (opens and clicks) for the first 24 hours after the campaign was sent.
  • Top links clicked
    The URLs that were clicked the most in the campaign.
  • Subscribers with most opens
    Subscribers that opened the campaign the most times.
  • Social performance
    Provides a birds-eye view of how well your campaign is doing across different social media outlets. When your campaign generates Facebook or campaign URL activity, we'll link to the stats on the report Overview. Click the links to view more detailed information about the social activity for your campaign.
  • Top locations
    Displays where in the world your subscribers are opening your campaigns. We use geolocation tracking to collect your subscribers' location information, and the name of the country subscribers are from.

When viewing the top-level, full campaign report, you can view comparable data, such as subscribers, opens, and clicks across each email in the entire campaign.  This can be seen below:

Using both the full campaign report and an individual email report, you can start to assess which emails are operating above the industry average and those that aren’t measuring up.  When reviewing these reports, it is important to consider the context of the emails in which they have been delivered. 

Email & Website Analytics Dashboard

In addition to the detailed MailChimp reports covered above, your Website Analytics Dashboard at your website provides a weekly snapshot of your key MailChimp metrics; Subscribers, Email's Sent, Opens, and Click Through.

Make sure you are monitoring your weekly results.

  1. Your Subscribers should be growing, adding new subscribers as some opt-out.
  2. Sending emails weekly, the sent emails are the total number sent to date.
  3. Opens, this is the total number of emails open to date.
  4. ClickThorugh is the total number of Click Through to date.

Email & Google Analytics

Referral Traffic to your website is measured through Direct and Email in Google Analytics > Acquisition > All Traffic > Channels. This report will provide the actual traffic to your site and how it performed. Email tracking via Google can be difficult because of how emails are tracked. You may see a report indicating Email. However, we often see the Email Traffic reporting in the Direct Source. Either way, check your results to make sure you have the desired impact and engagement.

 

Other Email Factors

Are there other extraneous factors that could be inhibiting the success of your email campaign?  Some of those factors are discussed below2.

  1. Is the trend in reporting a seasonal effect?

If you sell swimsuits and your campaigns see fewer openings in the winter, this is not abnormal.  It’s typical to see these types of fluctuations with seasonal products.  If the trend is not due to seasonality, then it could be something that you need to pay special attention to until it is discovered.

  1. Are there any anomalies?

Anomalies are when a metric dramatically rises or falls in your data.  They can alert you to both strong and poor performance, like when your message resonates well with consumers or if your message is off-target.  They can often also clue you in on extraneous outside factors that affect your results, so pay close attention to the peaks and valleys of your campaign report.  It would be best to determine whether these are outliers, something from the outside affecting the results, or inliers, things internally you are doing like subject lines, promos, or offers impacting your reader behavior.

  1. If you aren’t sure, could you run an A/B test?

Sometimes determining what is causing the peak or valley is hard to determine.  In this case, you should consider running an A/B test.  A/B Testing Campaigns allow you to test different versions of a single campaign to see how small changes can have a big impact on your results. Choose what you want to test, for example, the subject line or content, and compare results to find out what works and doesn't3.  To learn more about A/B Testing, specifically in MailChimp, click here.

Once you have clarity about what’s in your reports and the context of your specific email campaign, you can make smart and informed decisions about what to do next.

Let’s say you want to improve a metric that’s been the same for a long time. Using your reports, you can make an informed guess about what you could change to improve. Then, try making the change and tracking your results as a kind of experiment4:

  • Begin by coming up with a hypothesis about what will happen when you make a change.
  • Then test it.
  • Use your reports to determine whether the changes you are made working.
  • If it does, then you should keep replicating that action.
  • If not, test another element until you’ve determined what works.

The key to any testing is to make sure that you are using your marketing analytics to determine the value of each change.  It may take some trial and error, but with consistent monitoring and auditing of the process, you will find problematic areas for your email campaign for which you can improve.  Below is a list of these potential pitfalls and MailChimp sites that serve as prescriptions to these deficiencies:

MailChimp Email Resources

  1. Email Subject Line Titles: Choose your Words Wisely!
  2. How to Avoid Spam Filters
  3. How to Use Tags to Create Targeted Messages
  4. Create Groups for Segmented Targeting
  5. Design a Better Landing Page for Email Signups

 

References:

  1. MailChimp. About Email Campaign Reports. https://mailchimp.com/help/about-email-campaign-reports/
  2. MailChimp. Getting the Most Out of Your MailChimp Reports. https://mailchimp.com/resources/getting-the-most-out-of-your-mailchimp-reports/
  3. MailChimp. About A/B Testing Campaigns. https://mailchimp.com/help/about-ab-testing-campaigns/
  4. Same as #2

14.3 The Brand Axis

As we discussed in the previous section, the infinity loop represents the never-ending process of attracting and potentially repelling customers due to an individual’s or company’s marketing message, i.e., the inertia of the message magnet. As history has demonstrated, some marketing messages are well received and create highly charged magnetic responses. Like a real magnet, this polarized charge would draw in additional target audience consumers along the infinity loop. However, the infinity loop is not uni-directional, meaning it does not always flow unitarily in the same direction. The Social Media Magnet attracts from all paths along the infinity loop, as the consumers can be attracted to the message magnet from any direction. Likewise, a message that would repel consumers due to a poorly targeted message's decreased inertia can also push consumers away in any direction along the infinity loop. Therefore, the infinity loop provides the opportunity to orient multiple dimensions of impact upon the target market. Specifically, The Social Media Magnet theorizes both vertical and horizontal impacts upon the brand. This theoretical mapping of these axes is called the Brand Axis. The Brand Axis measures the loyalty and engagement of a target audience related to their own awareness of the brand in the landscape surrounding that brand.

Within the Brand Axis, the model theorizes the dimensional impact of “Loyalty” as represented by message awareness on the X-axis. Consumers on the far left of the axis have no loyalty due to being completely unaware of the message. In contrast, the consumers on the far right of the axis have no loyalty because they have completely forgotten the message. Note that both axis ends are not an ideal orientation to an individual or company relative to their marketing message. The ideal archetype for the loyalty dimension is directly in the center of the matrix, where the extensions of the infinity loop cross in the middle. However, in the middle ground between both endpoints and the center of the axis, there are varying degrees of awareness that can demarcate skepticism about the consumers’ awareness or forgetfulness of the brand. Consumers who would say, “Yeah, I think I have heard of that brand” or “Yes, I think I remember that brand” would qualify for this middle ground, representing a continuum of awareness on this X-axis.

Along the vertical Y-axis, the model theorizes the dimensional impact of “Engagement” as this consumer engagement is prevented due to extraneous forces on the brand message. At the top of the Y-axis, consumers are distracted from the marketing message due to environmental forces. At the bottom of the Y-axis, consumers are distracted from the marketing message due to competitive forces. Again, both the top and the bottom of the axis are not an ideal orientation on the plot, as the ideal is again directly in the center of the matrix, where the extensions of the infinity loop cross in the middle. Although, again, in the middle ground between both endpoints and the center of the axis, there are varying degrees of impact that these forces may have on the consumers’ level of engagement with the brand. Environmental impacts on consumers might lead them to say, “Yeah, I can’t afford that brand anymore,” or competitive impacts could direct them to express, “No, I like this other brand better.” These types of statements represent the continuum of engagement for the Y-axis.

Now that we have expounded on the nature of each axis let’s look at how they break up the Brand Axis into four quadrants that highlight different segments of consumers.  The four conceptual quadrants are labeled and described below:

Quadrant A: Unaware – Environmental

In this first quadrant, as consumers move further left, away from the Y-axis, they are increasingly unaware that the brand exists.  Those on the far left are completely unaware, while those closest to the Y-axis are, for the most part, aware of the brand, except for potentially the smallest of minor details.  In this quadrant, consumers are unaware due to environmental factors that can cloud their awareness.  Those closest to the top of the quadrant on the Y-axis are encountering a large number of distractions due to environmental concerns, while those closest to the X-axis are encountering very few environmental distractions.

Quadrant B: Forgotten – Environmental

In the second quadrant, as consumers move further, right away from Y-axis, they are perceived to be forgetting that the brand exists.  Those on the far right have completely forgotten, while those closest to the Y-axis are, for the most part, aware of the brand, except for forgetting the smallest of minor details.  In this quadrant, consumers have forgotten about the brand due to environmental factors that have clouded their memory.  Those closest to the top of the quadrant on the Y-axis are encountering a large number of distractions due to environmental concerns, while those closest to the X-axis are encountering very few environmental distractions.

Quadrant C: Forgotten – Competitive

In the third quadrant, as consumers move further, right away from Y-axis, they are perceived to be forgetting that the brand exists.  Those on the far right have completely forgotten, while those closest to the Y-axis are, for the most part, aware of the brand, except for forgetting the smallest of minor details.  Consumers have forgotten about the brand in this quadrant due to competitive factors that have clouded their memory.  Those closest to the top of the quadrant on the Y-axis are encountering a large number of distractions due to competitive factors, while those closest to the X-axis are encountering very few competitive distractions.

 Quadrant D: Unaware – Competitive

In the fourth and last quadrant, as consumers move further left, away from the Y-axis, they are increasingly unaware that the brand exists.  Those on the far left are completely unaware, while those closest to the Y-axis are, for the most part, aware of the brand, except for potentially the smallest of minor details.  In this quadrant, consumers are unaware due to competitive factors that can cloud their awareness.  Those closest to the top of the quadrant on the Y-axis are encountering a large number of distractions due to competitive concerns, while those closest to the X-axis are encountering very few competitive distractions.
title: 14.3 The Brand Axis

html:
14.4 The Strategic Impact of the Brand Axis

In The Social Media Magnet Theory, the perfect strategic brand alignment, called magnetic alignment, of the message magnet is centered over the intersection of the Loyalty (X-axis) and Engagement (Y-axis) on the Brand Axis.  At this point, the company’s (or individual’s) message magnet is also centered in the infinity loop, demonstrating that the brand elements align with the target market's desired perceptions.  The perfect alignment of the message magnet on the brand axis would like this:

In this perfect magnetic alignment, the target market consumers within the message magnet's boundaries (i.e., within the blue border of the message magnet above) are not part of the Brand Axis quadrants.  Because they are continually within reach of the brand’s targeted marketing messages, even though they may be on the edge of the boundary, there are no environmental or competitive forces acting strong enough on them to have them unaware or have forgotten about the brand.  In this ideal scenario, the message magnet is permanently centered right in the middle of the infinity loop. The loop is directly aligned at the center with the engagement and loyalty axes. Here, the marketing message is completely on-brand, and consumers on the infinity loop within the boundaries of the message magnet are the ideal target audience.  The message magnet will actually grow in size as the company (or individual) maintains this balance and grows its reach.  For example, as discussed in Chapter 2, Coke’s message magnet would nearly envelop the whole infinity loop as few consumers are unaware or have forgotten about Coca-Cola as a soft-drink choice. In contrast, new startup companies would have a very small message magnet on the Brand Axis.

Therefore, as these examples demonstrate, the Brand Axis acts as a map and compass for any company (or individual) running an inbound marketing campaign. Although while it would be ideal to have the message magnet centered on the Brand Axis permanently, numerous consulting opportunities in this domain have demonstrated to the author’s that it does not take long for the message magnet to become misaligned, or in other words, the message magnet can drift off the center of the loyalty and engagement axes. This event, called magnetic misalignment, can occur due to internal decisions (made within a company or by an individual) or external factors (occurrences out of the control of a company or an individual) that cause the message magnet to move off-center of the Brand Axis.  At times this might indicate that a company’s (or individual’s) marketing message is not being denoted correctly by the target audience or that the company’s marketing message is becoming off-target.  In this scenario, whether it is competitive or environmental factors contributing to this misalignment, it can happen quickly and is often hard to identify. For example, examine the following hypothetical scenario with the Brand Axis.

In this example, the message matrix has drifted directly left of the engagement axis into a neither environmentally nor competitively restrictive landscape. Therefore, this company’s messaging has attracted consumers who have never heard of the brand before. This is an acquisition strategy that has become misaligned, as the company is over-focused on new clients. This happens very frequently with some companies as they worry about growth. We would contend that at the same time, they are hypervigilant in attracting new customers. There are very loyal customers seeping out the back door of their strategy due to messaging efforts that do not speak to these loyal customers. For example, take a pop-up advertisement on a website that provides a 20% coupon off of a customer’s first order. While this may be appealing to signing up new customers for the first time, what does this indicate to loyal customers who purchase from the site often? Where is their 20% coupon, have they not earned it? Now, this is not to say that new acquisition strategies are not important. It just shouldn’t utilize the messaging space on the front of the website where loyal customers are certain to be perusing the site.

As you can see in this example, the brand axis is a monitoring tool for companies (and individuals) running social media campaigns regarding their message orientation. These authors contend that if and when a message magnet is determined to be misaligned, it should return to its key brand elements to re-center the message magnet.  We will explore these ideas further in the final chapter as we focus on the question: What happens when an individual or company’s message becomes misaligned?
title: 14.4 The Strategic Impact of the Brand Axis

html:
15.6 The Remedy to Magnetic Misalignment

Whether it is a misaligned push or pull scenario, companies (or individuals) that find themselves in any of these quadrants need to return to their four brand elements with a strategic intent to stay balanced between new and returning customers.  When considering the four brand elements, companies (or individuals) need to consider the following: the brand story, their brand promises, their brand beliefs, and brand trust. To bring the message magnet back into alignment, the brand must return to its original story to refocus the brand messages.

Much like a mission statement, the brand story requires that every other brand decision and brand message must build upon the story. In any future decision, if the outcome is in opposition to the brand story, then one should decide against it.  The story is about the personal journey that the company or individual has taken in creating the brand.  It can be about how the company (or individual) came up with the idea, product, or service. Or it could be metaphoric, and while it may not be an actual story, it would be a realistic narrative around the concept or idea. The story answers questions about the emotion, authenticity, and historical nature of the brand.  It helps identify who would want or need the brand and how it fulfills those desires.  The story lays the foundation for the brand promises that the individual or company will always uphold.

If the brand story is a mission statement, then the brand promise is the vision statement. What are those things that a company will promise to do for its customers, and how do they intend to keep this promise?  Brand promises give way to brand beliefs, which are the pillars of value that a company believes about the brand and attempts to convince their consumers to believe about the brand.  These values are built upon the foundation of the brand story and the brand promises, all combining together to invoke brand trust.  Brand trust is a personal relationship built over time as satisfaction by both parties, brand and consumer alike, is accomplished and repeated repeatedly.

A Shortcut for Remembering:

The reality is that when brands become misaligned, they more often push themselves into a magnetic misalignment than are being pushed by the landscape conditions around them.  It is, in fact, most often a misfortune of their own strategic misguided ways.  They lose sight of the key brand elements.  They become distracted and lose a grip on who they are and who their customers are, what they want, and how the company can provide it to them.  Yes, undoubtedly, the pull scenarios do occur. Still, in all of these instances, as demonstrated by each quadrant’s example, the hub is already naturally closer to the center of the Brand Axis.  The return to center is much easier in these situations as the company (or individual) has remained as centered as possible in the environmental and competitive pulls.  It is much faster and more likely that these companies will return to the center as soon as the landscape condition is alleviated. Still, for those misaligned push scenarios, those companies (or individuals) are voluntarily going deep into the quadrant due to internal strategic decisions.  The road to recovery is long and arduous as the center of the Brand Axis is almost at times unrecognizable, not only to you but to your target customers as well.

The Remedy to Magnetic Misalignment Is BRAND!

In conclusion, a company will never stay centered on the Brand Axis indefinitely.  There will always be decision opportunities that can and will move any company (or individual) off-center, off-brand into a misaligned state.  But the best way to prevent it as much as possible is to return to the brand elements continually.  Return to the process that established the inspiration for the brand in the first place.  If you keep the brand elements continually front and center, then we believe that not only will you stay centered in your brand messaging efforts, but over time you will start to see your message magnet grow and expand equally and dimensionally into all four quadrants of the Brand Axis.  Returning to an earlier example, we would point out a brand like Coca-Cola.  While its tagline may have changed over the years1 from “Have a Coke and a Smile” (1979), “Red, White, and You” (1986), “Life Taste’s Good” (2001), or “Open Happiness” (2009), the brand story is focused on sharing and togetherness2.  It unites people of all races, ages, economics, and tastes; it always has, and it always will.  As mentioned previously, this consistent message since 1886 has grown the message magnet on Coke’s Brand Axis to virtually cover the entire infinity loop, consistently holding the brand story as the focus of its message.  If you want your brand to become an icon, you will need to follow suit.

 

References:

  1. Coca-Cola Journey. A History of Coca-Cola Advertising Slogans.  https://www.coca-colacompany.com/stories/coke-lore-slogans
  2. We First. Coca-Cola On How Brand Story Shapes Brand Leadership.  https://www.wefirstbranding.com/brands/coca-cola-on-how-brand-story-shapes-brand-leadership/
title: 15.6 The Remedy to Magnetic Misalignment
